Whether your specific dependent category permits some study without changing status is not covered in these sources; confirm with USCIS or the school's DSO.

user_input: I'm an international student on F1 visa. What steps should I take to ensure I get a greencard in the next 10 years
reference: The Green Card process has three broad steps. First, determine which eligibility category fits you (for students this is commonly an employment-based category requiring an employer sponsor, or a family-based category). Second, in most categories a sponsor files an immigrant petition for you (Form I-140 for employment-based, Form I-130 for family-based). Third, when a visa number is available for your category and priority date, you apply for permanent residence: through adjustment of status (Form I-485) if you are in the United States, or consular processing abroad. Immediate-relative visas are always available, while preference categories depend on the Visa Bulletin. The sources describe this process but no strategy can guarantee a Green Card within 10 years.
reference_contexts: U.S. immigration laws provide a variety of ways for people to apply for a Green Card. The eligibility requirements may vary depending on the immigrant category you are applying under.
Adjustment of status is the process that you can use to apply for lawful permanent resident status (also known as applying for a Green Card) when you are present in the United States.
Immigrant visas for immediate relatives of U.S. citizens are unlimited, so they are always available.

user_input: What is O1 visa? How is it different from any other visa?
reference: The O-1 nonimmigrant visa is for individuals who possess extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics, or who have a demonstrated record of extraordinary achievement in the motion picture or television industry, recognized nationally or internationally. O-1A covers extraordinary ability in the sciences, education, business, or athletics; O-1B covers extraordinary ability in the arts or extraordinary achievement in film/TV. It differs from most other work visas in being based on the individual's demonstrated extraordinary ability rather than a job category or lottery; a U.S. petitioner files on the beneficiary's behalf, the initial period of stay is up to three years, and extensions are granted in increments of up to one year.
reference_contexts: The O-1 nonimmigrant visa is for the individual who possesses extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics, or who has a demonstrated record of extraordinary achievement in the motion picture or television industry and has been recognized nationally or internationally for those achievements.
Initial Period of Stay: Up to three years. Extension of Stay: We will determine the time you need to accomplish the initial event or activity in increments, up to one year.

user_input: I am not a US citizen. Can I get a Green Card or permanent residence if I marry a US citizen?
reference: Yes. The spouse of a U.S. citizen is an 'immediate relative,' and immigrant visas for immediate relatives of U.S. citizens are unlimited and always available. Your U.S. citizen spouse files an immigrant petition (Form I-130) for you; because a visa is immediately available to immediate relatives, if you are in the United States you may file Form I-485 (adjustment of status) concurrently with the I-130. If you are outside the United States you complete consular processing instead. You must otherwise be eligible, including having been lawfully admitted and having no disqualifying factors.
reference_contexts: Immigrant visas for immediate relatives of U.S. citizens are unlimited, so they are always available. Immediate relatives include: The spouses of U.S. citizens.
If you are an immediate relative, you can always concurrently file your Form I-485 application with the underlying Form I-130.

user_input: I graduated from my master's course. I'm still looking for jobs. How do I stop my unemployment days once my EAD arrives and I find a job?
reference: On post-completion OPT you may be unemployed for a limited number of days: up to 90 days on initial post-completion OPT, and an additional 60 days (150 total) if you receive the 24-month STEM OPT extension. Unemployment days stop accruing when you begin qualifying employment related to your area of study, and you may only start working once your EAD is valid. Report your employment to your Designated School Official (DSO) so your record is updated; STEM OPT students and their employers report employment and any material changes by submitting Form I-983 to the DSO.
reference_contexts: You may be unemployed during your OPT period for a limited number of days. If you received initial post-completion OPT only: up to 90 days. If you received the 24-month extension: an additional 60 days, for a total of 150 days during the OPT period.

user_input: There is a severe economic crisis happening in my home country which has blocked my funding. Can I taken an off-campus employment to support myself and is it illegal to do so?
reference: You may not simply start off-campus work: working in the United States without authorization is illegal and has serious consequences, including removal and reentry bars. However, F-1 students may be eligible for off-campus employment on a case-by-case basis in special situations such as severe economic hardship or special student relief. The employment must be authorized before you start any work, by your Designated School Official (DSO) and USCIS, and you generally request employment authorization by filing Form I-765 for an Employment Authorization Document. Speak with your DSO first.
reference_contexts: F-1 students may also be eligible to work off-campus on a case-by-case basis as a result of special situations such as severe economic hardship or special student relief. M-1 students may engage in practical training only after they have completed their studies. For both F-1 and M-1 students any off-campus training employment must be related to their area of study and must be authorized prior to starting any work by the Designated School Official (the person authorized to maintain the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS)) and USCIS.

Working in the United States without authorization has serious consequences, including removal from the country and reentry bars. Also, remaining in the United States in violation of your lawful nonimmigrant status could lead to an accrual of unlawful presence.
To request an EAD, you generally must file Form I-765, Application for Employment Authorization.

user_input: How many H-1B visas are available each year under the cap?
reference: Congress set the regular annual H-1B cap at 65,000 (the 'regular cap'). An additional 20,000 petitions filed for beneficiaries who earned a master's degree or higher from a U.S. institution are exempt from the regular cap (the 'master's cap'). Of the 65,000, up to 6,800 are set aside each fiscal year for the H-1B1 program under the U.S.-Chile and U.S.-Singapore free trade agreements, and unused H-1B1 numbers roll into the next fiscal year's regular cap. Not every H-1B petition is subject to the cap — some are cap-exempt.
reference_contexts: Congress set the current annual regular cap for the H-1B category at 65,000 (commonly known as the “regular cap”). Up to 6,800 visas are set aside from the 65,000 each fiscal year for the H-1B1 program under the terms of the legislation implementing the U.S.-Chile and U.S.-Singapore free trade agreements.
An additional 20,000 petitions filed on behalf of beneficiaries who have earned a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. institution of higher education are exempt from the cap.

user_input: My friend told me the H-1B selection is a purely random lottery. Is that how it still works?
reference: That description is outdated. Under the current process, if more registrations are received than there are cap numbers, USCIS runs a weighted selection among properly submitted registrations for unique beneficiaries, based generally on the highest OEWS wage level the beneficiary's proffered wage equals or exceeds. Registration is also counted per unique beneficiary rather than per filing — a beneficiary-centric change USCIS made under the 'Improving the H-1B Registration Selection Process and Program Integrity' final rule to reduce gaming. So it is still a selection among registrations, but not the simple random draw of earlier years.
reference_contexts: If a random selection process is necessary, USCIS will conduct a weighted selection among properly submitted registrations for unique beneficiaries based generally on the highest OEWS wage level that the beneficiary’s proffered wage will equal or exceed.
This is in large part because we implemented the beneficiary-centric selection process under the final rule Improving the H-1B Registration Selection Process and Program Integrity.

user_input: An old forum post said H-4 spouses are never allowed to work in the US. Is that true?
reference: Not as a blanket rule. Certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B workers can apply for employment authorization by filing Form I-765 — specifically if the H-1B spouse is the principal beneficiary of an approved Form I-140, or has been granted H-1B status under sections 106(a) and (b) of AC21. If approved, the H-4 spouse receives an EAD (Form I-766) and may work through its expiration date; they are not authorized to work until USCIS approves the Form I-765. So H-4 spouses who don't meet those conditions cannot work, but the categorical 'never' is incorrect.
reference_contexts: Certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B nonimmigrants can file Form I-765, Application for Employment Authorization, if the H-1B nonimmigrant: Is the principal beneficiary of an approved Form I-140, Immigrant Petition for Alien Worker; or Has been granted H-1B status under sections 106(a) and (b) of the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-first Century Act of 2000
